newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mobutu opposes talks with rebels - spokesman.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu opposes talks with rebels - spokesman.

text.p: Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko flatly opposes talks with rebel forces who control a swathe of eastern Zaire and have vowed to overthrow him, his son and spokesman said on Monday.
"The Zairean government and President Mobutu seek the withdrawal, pure and simple, of all foreign troops from Zairean territory," Mobutu spokesman Mobutu Nzanga told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Zaire says the rebel forces led by Laurent Kabila are backed by soldiers from Burundi, Rwanda and Uganda.
Mobutu has been at his villa on the French Riviera since last Friday, where has spent time at regular intervals since prostate cancer surgery last August.
The younger Mobutu said his father, who has been president for 31 years, had opposed negotiating with the rebels from the outset of the uprising and still clung to that view.
He added that he was unaware of any talks, direct or indirect, under way between Zaire and representatives of the rebellion.
Nor were any contacts planned between rebel leaders and Mobutu while the Zairean head of state was at his villa in Roquebrune-Cap Martin.
South African officials, who have been trying to promote talks between the two sides, also said on Monday that no discussions were under way at the moment.
"There is pressure. Some governments want Zaire to have talks, but it is not in our interest," Mobutu Nzanga said.

"They want us to discuss the departure of President Mobutu," he said, referring to the rebels. "They are not setting us a democratic example by killing people and enrolling 10- to 15-year-old kids (in their army)," he said.
France, meanwhile, said it was extremely worried by a recent resumption of the fighting in eastern Zaire as rebel forces mounted a new drive on the eastern town of Kalima.
"We urgently appeal for a halt in the hostilities," Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt told reporters in Paris.
The rebels have advanced quickly from the east on several fronts, blunting an army counter-offensive launched from Zaire's third city of Kisangani on January 20.
South African President Nelson Mandela said on Monday that he and other African leaders would meet President Mobutu on March 19 in a new bid to end the uprising.
Mandela said negotiators would deal separately with Kabila.
Last week Mandela announced plans for the warring sides to get together for talks in Cape Town, but was criticised for letting the cat out of the bag when they failed to take place.
Kabila nonetheless said at the weekend he would delay a planned offensive to give the latest peace initiative a chance.
